prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Anita Dunham's first heart attack started with a mysterious pain in her arm -- and, suddenly, the 34-year-old felt as if she couldn't breathe. After she got dressed, she could barely speak because the pain was so great in her arms and chest. Jolen Johnson took this photo of co-workers wearing red Friday in Cedar Park, Texas. Dunham, who had a second heart attack in 2002, wore red Friday to spread awareness about heart disease. Now 64 years old, she said she wants women everywhere to know that heart disease, the No. 1 killer for women, can affect women in all walks of life. She and others shared their stories with CNN's iReport.com. Read more about Dunham . The National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, part of the National Institutes of Health, promoted the red clothing day to spread the message that "Heart Disease Doesn't Care What You Wear -- It's the #1 Killer of Women," according to its Web site. Others who wore red have family members who succumbed to heart disease. Robin Savage, 42, of San Juan Capistrano, California, said her grandfather, father and mother all had heart disease. Besides wearing red herself, she goes to heart events and takes pictures of them for a local Web site.  See more from iReporters on National Wear Red Day » . Savage has to take beta blockers because her heart sometimes races when she eats certain things, particularly foods containing the preservative MSG. She watches her diet closely and exercises 30 minutes a day to keep herself healthy. iReport.com: Heart Disease runs in my family . For her sons, 9 and 12, she monitors their diet closely, but fears that she will die while they are young. "It's such a huge void in your life, especially when you have your own kids and you don't have your mom around to, say, ask questions," she said. "I was completely lost when I had kids." Visit CNNhealth.com, your connection to better living . Peggy Roesch, a 24-year-old graphic designer from Cincinnati, Ohio, said her grandfather had a heart attack five years ago. She was recently inspired by her mother, who runs marathons, to start running more herself. iReport.com: Seeing red . Eileen Velez from West Palm Beach, Florida, has been organizing her co-workers to wear red to show heart awareness every year since 2007. "If everyone is wearing red at the same time, somebody is going to notice," she said. iReport.com: Kimley-Horn and Associates . Despite the nationwide movement, Dunham said she hadn't noticed anyone else in her town of Earlimart, California, wearing red on Friday. Her message to others at risk for heart disease is to watch their weight. "I tell [my daughter] every day, 'You know you need to start watching your diet or you're going to be in the hospital with a heart attack,'" she said. CNN's Cristina Martin contributed to this report.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Anita Dunham was 34 when she suffered her first heart attack. It began as an unexplained ache in one arm, followed by the sudden sensation that she could not breathe. By the time she had put on her clothes, the pain in her chest and arms was so severe that speaking was nearly impossible.

Dunham experienced another heart attack in 2002. Now 64, she participated in Friday’s red-clothing campaign to raise awareness of heart disease. She wants women from every background to understand that the condition can affect anyone and is the leading cause of death among women.

Dunham and other participants told their stories through CNN’s iReport.com. Read more about Dunham.

In Cedar Park, Texas, Jolen Johnson photographed colleagues dressed in red on Friday.

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, which is part of the National Institutes of Health, promoted the day. According to its website, the campaign carried the message: “Heart Disease Doesn’t Care What You Wear — It’s the #1 Killer of Women.”

Some participants wore red in memory of relatives who died from heart disease.

Robin Savage, 42, of San Juan Capistrano, California, said the disease affected her grandfather, her father and her mother. In addition to dressing in red, Savage attends heart-related events and photographs them for a local website.

See more iReporter coverage of National Wear Red Day.

Savage takes beta blockers because certain foods—especially those containing the preservative MSG—sometimes cause her heart to race. To protect her health, she carefully manages what she eats and exercises for 30 minutes each day.

iReport.com: Heart disease runs in my family.

She also closely supervises the diets of her two sons, ages 9 and 12. Savage worries that she could die while they are still young.

Losing her own mother left an enormous absence in her life, she said, particularly after she became a parent and no longer had her mother available to answer questions. When she had children, Savage said, she felt completely adrift.

Visit CNNhealth.com, your resource for healthier living.

Peggy Roesch, a 24-year-old graphic designer in Cincinnati, Ohio, said her grandfather suffered a heart attack five years earlier. More recently, her marathon-running mother motivated her to begin running more often.

iReport.com: Seeing red.

Eileen Velez of West Palm Beach, Florida, has encouraged her colleagues to wear red in support of heart-health awareness every year since 2007. She said that when everyone dresses in red simultaneously, someone is bound to take notice.

iReport.com: Kimley-Horn and Associates.

Although the campaign took place across the country, Dunham said she did not see anyone else wearing red Friday in her community of Earlimart, California.

Her advice to people vulnerable to heart disease is to keep a close eye on their weight. Dunham said she warns her daughter every day that she must begin paying attention to her diet or she could eventually be hospitalized after a heart attack.

CNN’s Cristina Martin contributed to the report.
outputs.L3:
Anita Dunham suffered her first heart attack at just 34 years old and experienced a second one in 2002. By wearing red, she hoped to raise awareness that heart disease is the leading cause of death among women and can affect women of every background.

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute promoted National Wear Red Day as part of an effort to educate the public about women’s heart disease. Women such as Robin Savage participated in awareness events to emphasize the importance of prevention and early action. Because Savage has a strong family history of heart disease, she takes medication, follows a healthy diet, and exercises daily to manage her own risk factors.

Savage is also careful about what her sons eat because she worries about their long-term heart health. Given her family’s medical history, she fears that heart disease could cause her to die while her children are still young. Her concerns underscore the importance of awareness, healthy habits, and preventive care for women and their families.
outputs.L4:
Women living with heart disease, along with their families and supporters, marked National Wear Red Day by wearing red, sharing personal experiences, and encouraging others to take heart health seriously. The annual observance raises awareness of cardiovascular disease in women and highlights the importance of prevention, early detection, and timely medical care.

Participants emphasized that heart disease does not affect only older adults or people with a particular lifestyle. Women of any age, race, or background can be at risk, and symptoms may not always match the classic warning signs commonly associated with a heart attack. In addition to chest pain, women may experience shortness of breath, nausea, unusual fatigue, dizziness, or discomfort in the back, neck, jaw, or arms. Recognizing these symptoms and seeking immediate help can save lives.

Families affected by heart disease also spoke about the emotional impact of diagnosis and recovery. Their stories served as reminders that knowing one’s family history, attending regular medical checkups, and monitoring blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar can help identify risks before a serious event occurs.

Prevention was a central message of the day. Health advocates encouraged women to eat a balanced diet, exercise regularly, avoid smoking, manage stress, get adequate sleep, and follow medical advice. Even small, consistent changes can improve cardiovascular health over time.

By wearing red and speaking openly about their experiences, participants hoped to inspire more women to pay attention to their bodies and make heart health a priority. Their message was clear: heart disease remains the leading cause of death among women, but greater awareness, healthy habits, and early action can reduce the risk and improve outcomes.

**(Health Desk) —** The first warning came while Maya Reynolds was carrying groceries into her apartment. A dull ache spread from her shoulder to her jaw, followed by nausea and an exhaustion so sudden that she sat down on the kitchen floor.

At 36, Reynolds assumed she was stressed. She had no crushing chest pain—the symptom she associated with a heart attack—and decided to rest rather than seek help.

By the next morning, she could barely climb the stairs.

Doctors at a nearby emergency department discovered that Reynolds had experienced a heart attack. The diagnosis stunned her family, but cardiovascular specialists say her experience illustrates a dangerous misconception: Heart disease does not affect only older adults, and its warning signs are not always dramatic.

Women can experience chest pressure during a heart attack, but they may also report shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, unusual fatigue, or pain in the back, arm, neck or jaw. Because these symptoms can resemble anxiety, indigestion or overexertion, patients may delay treatment.

That delay can have serious consequences. When blood flow to part of the heart is blocked, heart muscle begins to sustain damage. Prompt treatment can restore circulation and improve the chances of recovery.

Risk factors include high blood pressure, elevated cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, obesity and a family history of cardiovascular disease. Pregnancy-related complications, autoimmune conditions and early menopause may also affect a woman’s long-term risk.

Reynolds underwent a procedure to open a narrowed artery and later began cardiac rehabilitation. She now takes medication, exercises under medical supervision and pays closer attention to symptoms she once would have dismissed.

“I thought I was too young,” she said. “Now I know that age doesn’t make you immune.”

Health professionals advise calling emergency services immediately when heart-attack symptoms are suspected. Patients should not drive themselves or wait for the discomfort to disappear.

For Reynolds, recovery has included more than physical healing. It has meant reconsidering what a heart attack looks like—and sharing that lesson with others.

“If something feels seriously wrong, don’t talk yourself out of getting help,” she said. “It’s better to be checked and be wrong than to stay home and lose time.”
